ended: Lost the East Finals 0-4 to NY

archetype.name: Contender That Fell Short (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A 52-win team with a top-six offense and a merely average defense that won two seven-game series, including one over the division-winning Pistons, then was swept in the East Finals.

report.headline: Fewer wins than last year, deeper into May, then a hard stop against New York

recap.finish: 52-30, second in the Central; beat TOR 4-3 and DET 4-3, lost the East Finals 0-4 to NY
recap.body:
This was a step back from the 64-18 juggernaut of a year ago that still ended with more playoff wins than any Cavaliers season in the sheet's history. The regular-season profile slipped across the board. Net Rtg fell from 9.5 to 4.1 (9th). The offense went from 1st to 6th, and the defense sat 15th, rating 115.1 against a league average of 115.7. The record was earned rather than lucky: W vs Pt Diff of 1 and 51 wins implied by the margin.

The season started flat. They were 3-3 in October and 7-7 in December, which left them 19-16 just before the new year. From January on they were a different team: 10-5, then an 8-3 February in which they allowed only 110 points a game, then 10-5 in March and 5-1 in April. The longest skid all year was three games. It wasn't enough to catch Detroit at 60-22, but they finished the regular season playing like the contender they had been a year earlier.

The engine was the backcourt and the two bigs. Donovan Mitchell ranked 1st of 144 shooting guards, made All-NBA Second Team and led the team in Win Shares with a +6.9 On-Off. James Harden (8th of 89 at point guard, 7.7 Win Shares) gave them a second high-usage creator. Evan Mobley (5th of 93) and Jarrett Allen (66.9 TS %) anchored a B frontcourt. What slipped was the shooting. 3P % fell from 38.3 to 36.0, essentially league average, even as the team kept firing at a top-ten 3PA Rate. On the other end, opponents hit 37.2% from three, 26th in the league. The wings were the soft spot: a C+ group in which Max Strus played only 12 games, and as a result small forwards barely registered in the rotation's minutes.

The playoffs showed how good and how thin this team was. Toronto took them seven games before a 114-102 home win closed it out. Then they went into Detroit for Game 7 and won 125-94 to beat the division champion. New York ended it quickly. Game 1 was lost in overtime and Games 2 and 3 by double digits, and Game 4 was a 130-93 blowout. Across 18 games the offense scored 107.94 a game against 119.52 in the regular season. TOV % of 15.1 ranked 15th of 16 playoff teams, and Mitchell's TS % dropped from 61.3 to 55.8. Two wars of attrition left nothing for the third round.

The year leaves a core that clearly works and a pair of problems that are just as clear. The offense needs its shooting back. The defense has to stop leaking threes. Both point to the wing group the roster never really had.

highlights.title: Two seven-game series wins
highlights.body: They outlasted Toronto and then beat 60-win Detroit, finishing with a 31-point Game 7 road win. The 8 playoff wins rank 4th in the league and are the most for this franchise in the sheet's history, after peaks of 5 the two previous years. It shows the top of this roster can win playoff series, not just regular-season games.

highlights.title: Mitchell as the best shooting guard
highlights.body: Mitchell topped the site's shooting guard tab and made All-NBA Second Team. The team was far better with him on the floor than off it. His scoring efficiency held up at a high usage rate, which is why the offense stayed top-six even after the shooting regressed. That level is repeatable as long as he is healthy.

highlights.title: Second-half surge, honestly earned
highlights.body: After a .500 December they won steadily from January through April, and the February defense was the best stretch of the year. The final record matches the point differential almost exactly, so the improvement came from outscoring opponents, not from close-game luck.

lowlights.title: The East Finals collapse
lowlights.body: New York swept them, and only the overtime opener was close. The offense fell well below its regular-season level over the playoffs, and turnovers ballooned to near the bottom of the playoff field. The deep series beforehand likely mattered, but the Knicks exposed a team that couldn't generate clean offense once Mitchell and Harden were contained.

lowlights.title: Perimeter defense leaked threes
lowlights.body: Opponents shot 37.2% from three, 26th in the league, and the overall defense was only average. A year ago it ranked 8th. Small forwards in particular hit more threes against Cleveland than against anyone. That fits a roster with almost no healthy wing depth, and it will persist until the position is filled.

lowlights.title: A wing group in name only
lowlights.body: The wings graded C+. Strus, the main small forward, played 12 regular-season games, and the listed wings combined for a sliver of the minutes the backcourt and frontcourt logged. Dennis Schröder's inefficient minutes (52.6 TS %, -2.2 BPM) filled part of the gap and didn't help.

arc.note: A .500 team into the new year, they won consistently from January on and carried it through two Game 7 wins before the Knicks ended it abruptly.

recap.nextYear: The four players who carried the year are the foundation: Mitchell, Harden, Mobley and Allen, all ranked near the top of their position tabs with strong Win Shares. That foundation earned its record rather than lucking into it, so a 50-win baseline looks real. The two things that dropped them from 64 wins to 52 are specific. The 3P % fell back to league average from last year's 38.3, and that may partly recover. Opponents' three-point shooting ranked near the bottom of the league and won't fix itself. Both trace back to the wings, the one group graded below a B and the one that barely played. The playoff turnover spike and the stars' efficiency drop say the offense needs a creator beyond its two guards, and Schröder's numbers say that player isn't already on the roster."
